items.title: Merton's strain typology
items.claim: Robert Merton (1938) argued that crime arises when cultural goals exceed legitimate means. How many adaptations did he identify?
items.reveal:
Merton's 1938 essay 'Social Structure and Anomie' set out five responses to the gap between goals and means.

The theory has been extended by Agnew (1992) into General Strain Theory.
items.why: Strain theory still underpins much policy thinking about inequality and crime.

items.title: Becker's central claim
items.claim: Howard Becker's Outsiders (1963) argued that deviance is not a quality of the act but of the social response. Which statement summarises his view?

options.text: Deviance is created by groups that make rules and apply them to others
Deviance is identical across all societies

items.reveal_title: The labelled act is created by the labellers
items.reveal:
Becker wrote that 'social groups create deviance by making the rules whose infraction constitutes deviance'.

His fieldwork with jazz musicians and marijuana users in 1950s Chicago shaped symbolic interactionism in criminology.
items.why: Labelling theory shifted sociological focus from offenders to the institutions that define offence.

items.title: Durkheim's 1897 finding
items.claim: In Le Suicide (1897), Emile Durkheim argued that suicide rates depend on social, not individual, factors. Which pattern did he report?

options.text: Catholics had higher rates than Protestants
Protestants had higher rates than Catholics, and the unmarried higher than the married
No religious or marital differences existed
Rates were identical across all European countries

items.reveal_title: Group integration mattered more than personal pathology
items.reveal:
Durkheim correlated rates with degree of social integration. Higher integration (Catholic, married, wartime) tended to predict lower rates.

Later critics (Douglas, 1967) questioned the reliability of historical suicide records.
items.why: Durkheim's argument founded sociology as a discipline studying 'social facts' independent of individual minds.
